plot.label: Graph of the velocity v(t) in meters per second for t from 0 to 10 seconds, made of segments through (0, 0), (2, 4), (5, 4), (8, -2) and (10, -2)
Graph of the velocity v(t) = 4 - t + 2 sin t in feet per second for t from 0 to 6 seconds, positive at first and negative near the end

items.q: Find the displacement of the particle from $t = 0$ to $t = 10$ seconds. Include units.

mistakes.why: That adds every area as positive: it is the total distance. Displacement subtracts the areas below the axis: $4 + 12 + 4 - 1 - 4$.
Count every piece: the triangle above the axis on (5, 7) adds 4 and the one below on (7, 8) subtracts 1.

items.q: Find the total distance the particle travels from $t = 0$ to $t = 10$ seconds. Include units.

mistakes.why: That is the displacement. Distance counts the leftward motion too: $4 + 12 + 4 + 1 + 4$.

items.q: The particle is at $x = -3$ meters at $t = 0$. Find its position at $t = 10$.

mistakes.why: That is the displacement. Add it to the starting position: $-3 + 15$.
$x(10) = x(0) + 15 = -3 + 15$; the starting position is negative.

items.q: At what time on $[0, 10]$ is the particle farthest to the right, and why?
options: $t = 5$: $v$ starts to decrease there.
$t = 7$: $v$ changes from positive to negative there.
$t = 10$: the position has had the most time to grow.
$t = 2$: $v$ reaches its maximum value there.

why.correct: $x' = v$ changes from positive to negative at $t = 7$, so $x$ has a relative maximum there, and $x(7) = 17$ beats $x(0) = -3$ and $x(10) = 12$.
options: After $t = 5$ the particle still moves right, more slowly, until $t = 7$.
The particle moves right until $t = 7$ and left after it; $x(7) = -3 + 20 = 17$ is the largest.
From $t = 7$ on the particle moves left, so $x(10) = 12 < x(7)$.
The fastest moment is not the farthest point.

items.q: On which interval is the particle speeding up?

why.correct: Speeding up needs $v$ and $a$ with the same sign. On $(7, 8)$ both are negative (and on $(0, 2)$ both are positive).
options: There $v < 0$ and $a = v' = -2 < 0$: same signs.
$v > 0$ but $a < 0$: the particle slows down.
$a = 0$ there: the speed stays 2 m/s.
$a = 0$ there: the speed stays 4 m/s.

items.q: A particle moves with velocity $v(t) = 4 - t + 2\sin t$ feet per second, $0 \le t \le 6$. Find its displacement on $[0, 6]$. Include units.

mistakes.why: That is the total distance. Displacement is $\int_0^6 v(t)\,dt$, without absolute value.

items.q: Find the total distance the particle travels on [0, 6]. Include units.

mistakes.why: That is the displacement: the leftward motion after $t \approx 3.430$ was subtracted. Use $\int_0^6 |v(t)|\,dt$.

items.q: At $t = 0$ the particle is at $x = 5$ feet. Find its position at $t = 6$.

mistakes.why: Position uses the displacement, not the total distance.

items.q: Is the particle speeding up or slowing down at $t = 5$?
options: Speeding up: $v(5) < 0$ and $a(5) < 0$.
Slowing down: $a(5) < 0$.
Slowing down: $v(5)$ and $a(5)$ have opposite signs.
Speeding up: $v(5) > 0$ and $a(5) > 0$.

why.correct: $v(5) \approx -2.918$ and $a(5) = v'(5) \approx -0.433$ have the same sign, so the speed is increasing (radian mode).
options: A negative acceleration slows the particle only when $v > 0$; here $v(5) < 0$ too.
Both are negative at $t = 5$.
$v(5) \approx -2.918$ and $a(5) \approx -0.433$, both negative.

items.q: Which expression gives the total distance a particle with velocity $v(t)$ travels from $t = 1$ to $t = 4$?
options: $\left|\int_1^4 v(t)\,dt\right|$

why.correct: Total distance $= \int_1^4 |v(t)|\,dt$; the absolute value goes inside the integral.
options: That is the size of the displacement; back-and-forth motion cancels inside.
That is the displacement.
That is $v(4) - v(1)$, a change in velocity.
The integral of speed counts every stretch as positive.

items.q: A particle has velocity $v(t) = 3t^2 - 2$ and position $x(1) = 4$. Find $x(t)$.

mistakes.why: This has $x(1) = -1$. Add the constant that makes $x(1) = 4$.
That starts the integral at $t = 0$. $x(t) = 4 + \int_1^t (3s^2 - 2)\,ds = t^3 - 2t + 5$.
That is the acceleration, the derivative of v. Position is an antiderivative of v.

items.q: A particle moves with $v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3$ m/s. Find the total distance it travels on $0 \le t \le 4$, without a calculator.

mistakes.why: That is $\int_0^4 v(t)\,dt$, the displacement. Split at $t = 1$ and $t = 3$, where $v$ changes sign.

why.correct: $v = (t - 1)(t - 3)$ changes sign at 1 and 3. $\int_0^1 v = \frac{4}{3}$, $\int_1^3 v = -\frac{4}{3}$, $\int_3^4 v = \frac{4}{3}$. Total distance $= 4$ m.

items.q: For the same particle, $v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3$ m/s, find the displacement on $0 \le t \le 4$.

mistakes.why: That is the total distance. Displacement keeps the sign: $\frac{4}{3} - \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3}$.

items.q: For a particle with velocity $v(t)$ in m/s, $\int_2^5 |v(t)|\,dt = 9$. What does this mean?
options: At t = 5 the particle is 9 meters from where it was at t = 2.
At t = 5 the speed of the particle is 9 meters per second.
At t = 5 the particle is at the point x = 9 meters.
The particle travels 9 meters between t = 2 and t = 5 seconds, counting both directions.

why.correct: $\int_2^5 |v(t)|\,dt$ is the total distance traveled from $t = 2$ to $t = 5$ seconds, in meters.
options: That is the displacement, $\int_2^5 v(t)\,dt$, which may be smaller.
An integral of speed is a distance, in meters.
The integral is a change, not a position.
The integral of speed is the total distance.

items.q: A particle has acceleration $a(t) = 6t$ m/s² and velocity $v(0) = -3$ m/s. Find $v(2)$.

mistakes.why: That is $\int_0^2 6t\,dt$, the change in velocity. Add $v(0) = -3$.
$v(2) = v(0) + 12 = -3 + 12$; the initial velocity is negative.

items.q: A particle's velocity $v$ is continuous and $\int_0^6 v(t)\,dt = 0$, with $v$ not 0 on the whole interval. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: $v$ changes sign somewhere in $(0, 6)$.
The total distance traveled is 0.
The particle is at rest at $t = 3$.

why.correct: $\int_0^6 v = x(6) - x(0) = 0$; motion right and left cancel, so $v$ changes sign, but the distance is positive.
options: Zero displacement: it ends where it started.
If $v$ kept one sign and were not 0 throughout, the integral could not be 0.
Distance is $\int_0^6 |v(t)|\,dt > 0$ when the particle moves.
The integral says nothing about when $v = 0$.
